title: Plausible Stories Are Not Explanations
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen examines the question of whether AI-generated video can improve learning, and uses it as a case study in how educators mistake plausible mechanisms for actual explanations. Drawing on David Deutsch's criterion that a good explanation must be 'hard to vary' — its components cannot be changed without breaking the explanation — Allen argues that most claims about educational technology offer stories that are easy to vary, and therefore are not genuine explanations at all. She applies Höffler and Leutner's meta-analysis, which found a strong effect of animation for spatial/procedural content (d=1.06) but near-zero effects for declarative content, to show that 'video is engaging' explains nothing. She closes with a warning about the fluency trap: as AI lowers the production cost of educational video, the volume of plausible-but-untested material will increase, and educators will need stronger epistemic standards to resist it.
points: Deutsch's 'hard to vary' test distinguishes real explanations from plausible stories: a genuine explanation's components are tightly coupled so that changing any one of them breaks the explanation. Most edtech claims fail this test.

Höffler and Leutner's meta-analysis found animation produces a large effect for spatial and procedural content (d=1.06) but near-zero effects for declarative content — demonstrating that 'video is engaging' is not an explanation, because the effect depends entirely on what type of content is being taught.
The fluency trap: AI makes high-quality video trivially cheap to produce, which will flood classrooms with polished, confident-seeming material that has never been tested against learning outcomes.
When we accept a plausible mechanism as an explanation, we remove the question from scrutiny — and the damage is done not by the mechanism being wrong but by our stopping the inquiry.
Educators need a working theory of what kind of content benefits from what kind of medium, based on evidence — not a general prior that 'more engaging format = more learning.'
quotes: A plausible story is not an explanation. An explanation must be hard to vary — you cannot change its components without breaking it. Most claims about educational technology are easy to vary, which is a sign they are not actually explaining anything.
Höffler and Leutner found a large effect for spatial content and almost nothing for declarative content. 'Video is engaging' does not explain that pattern. An actual explanation would.

The fluency trap is the real danger. As AI makes polished educational video trivially cheap, we will be flooded with content that feels authoritative because it looks professional. Feeling authoritative is not the same as working.
We are not short of plausible mechanisms in education. We are short of mechanisms that are hard to vary — that make predictions specific enough to be falsifiable.
